extracted.intended_audience: scientists, philosophers, and students studying the logic of scientific method and inductive reasoning
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for detecting and avoiding common fallacies in scientific reasoning, especially errors in a priori inference, observation, and generalization. Focuses on how to observe, record, and infer correctly to support sound induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject the maxim 'Tout ce qui est vrai de l’effet, est vrai de la cause.'
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not assume that properties of an effect must also be properties of its cause (i.e., 'Tout ce qui est vrai de l’effet, est vrai de la cause').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This a priori inference is fallacious except in narrow/technical senses. Examples and historical instances include Victor Cousin's unqualified maxim, Coleridge's claim that causality holds only between homogeneous things, Spinoza's and Descartes' related deductions, and Leibnitz’s pre-established harmony and Malebranche’s occasional causes. Beware inferences that deduce qualities of causes (including theological attributes) directly from observed effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using presumed divine perfection or a priori beliefs to override empirical evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not let appeals to the perfection, goodness, or presumed qualities of a deity (or other a priori suppositions) be used as an argument against observed facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: opposing empirical theories by arguing they would be a reflection on the goodness or wisdom of the Deity (e.g., using divine benevolence to reject the principle of population). Such arguments are a form of 'a priori' fallacy and are unreliable fencing-off devices; they should not substitute for observation and experiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify observation errors as Non-observation or Mal-observation
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation fallacies split into two kinds: Non-observation (overlooking facts or circumstances) and Mal-observation (seeing something wrongly — mistaking inference for perception).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these categories to diagnose observational defects: Non-observation covers both overlooking instances and overlooking material circumstances; Mal-observation primarily involves conflating inference with direct perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-observation — overlooking instances
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-observation is when one overlooks or neglects facts or particulars that ought to have been observed; specifically, overlooking instances relevant to a hypothesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selective memory and attention (remembering confirming instances and forgetting failures) create this fallacy: e.g., credit given to fortune-tellers or almanac-makers because people remember hits, not misses. Remedy: seek and record all instances, actively look for counterexamples, and apply the elimination-of-chance logic (anticipate how many coincidences are expected by chance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-observation — overlooking circumstances (confounders)
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-observation of material circumstances in observed instances — important contextual factors are missed, producing false conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: collusion in fulfilled prophecies, phlogiston theory failing because gaseous combustion products were not observed, 'sympathetic powder' cures that omitted concurrent dressings/rest that actually healed. Remedy: explicitly enumerate and control for all relevant circumstances and concurrent interventions; investigate and report hidden/omitted factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preconceived opinion as the greatest cause of non-observation
rubrics_metrics.description: A preconceived theory or opinion often causes observers to miss facts contradictory to that theory, even if such facts are directly observable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manifest in travel reports, religious readings, and historical writing (observers see what they expect). Countermeasure: cultivate skeptical self-awareness of prior beliefs, design observations/experiments specifically aimed to test against your expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use simple experiments to test intuitive objections (don't rely on intuition alone)
rubrics_metrics.description: When an objection can be resolved by a simple empirical test, perform the test instead of relying on intuition or armchair reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration: the Copernican objection about a dropped stone (mast vs tower) would have been settled by simple experiment. Whenever feasible, translate disputes into direct, reproducible tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value negative instances highly when forming axioms
rubrics_metrics.description: Negative instances (failures, counterexamples) are especially powerful evidence for constructing or refuting axioms — they often carry more weight than affirmative instances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted principle: 'in omni Axiomate vero constituendo, major vis est instantiæ negativæ.' Actively seek and record negative evidence rather than only collecting confirming cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mistaking inference for perception (Mal-observation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not conflate what is directly perceived by the senses with the inferences or hypotheses drawn from those perceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: resistance to the Copernican system arose from confusing apparent motion with direct visual perception; witnesses and lay observers commonly mix hypothesis into their reports. Remedy: when reporting or evaluating observations, separate raw sensory data from interpretive inferences; train analytic habits or use cross-examination and careful note-taking to isolate perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against generalization from insufficient or biased samples (Fallacies of Generalization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Generalizations made from insufficient, improperly selected, or biased instances (inductive mistakes committed on principle) are fallacies of generalization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish casual lapses from principled misconceptions of induction. Avoid 'per enumerationem simplicem' (simple enumeration) generalizations that do not seek decisive instances; ensure sampling and elimination-of-chance criteria satisfy the standards laid out for sound induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for expected coincidences (elimination of chance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that some coincidences are expected by chance and that people naturally over-remember surprising coincidences, leading to false inferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an apparent pattern or successful prediction could be a random coincidence, calculate or consider how many coincidences of that kind are likely to occur by chance; do not attribute causal power without eliminating chance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize limits of untrained observational faculties and use trained methods when necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinary sensory faculties, even when habitually exercised, can fail to yield exact knowledge; subtle or complex phenomena may require trained, systematic observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: painters must train to perceive color/shape details; chemists discovered gaseous combustion residues only after directed inquiry. Remedy: apply appropriate instruments, training, and systematic methods when precise observation is needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider timing and tempo of effects when attributing efficacy
rubrics_metrics.description: When judging whether an intervention caused an effect, consider whether the timing and natural course of the phenomenon make the purported cause plausible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: yellow fever victims may die before a slow-acting treatment could take effect (so absence of deaths after treatment may reflect survivorship bias), or rest/regimen rather than a remedy may explain recovery (John Wesley example). Analyze temporal plausibility and natural histories before assigning causation.
